```{=html}
<h1 class="gw-chapter-title">How does a pumping impact become a management decision?</h1>
</div>
```

:::: gw-chapter-intro
::: gw-chapter-intro__body
::: gw-prose
Pumping groundwater near a stream depletes it — by drawing surface water
into the aquifer or by intercepting groundwater that would have fed the
stream. The effect is lagged and depends on aquifer properties that are
usually inferred rather than observed, which makes interconnected surface
water (ISW) one of the hardest quantities to account for under SGMA.

All {{< var active_basins_word >}} subbasins run a numerical
groundwater–surface water model, and none uses model output directly as
its compliance measure. Compliance runs instead on groundwater levels or
streamflow at monitoring sites — a proxy for the depletion itself.
:::
:::

<h2 class="gw-eyebrow">The accounting chain</h2>
<p class="gw-section-lede">Seven steps connect a pumping well to a management decision. The chain holds through modelling — and breaks where compliance switches to a proxy.</p>

<section class="gw-steps-scene isw-scene" data-scroll-steps aria-label="The interconnected surface water accounting chain, step by step">
  <div class="gw-steps-scene__figure">
    <figure class="gw-figure isw-figwrap" data-follow>
      <p id="isw-plate-summary" class="gw-sr-summary">
            A shallow cutaway of a stream and the ground beneath it. A thick band
            of vegetation sits over a thicker band of brown sediment; below them
            is one continuous saturated aquifer. The boundary between the brown
            sediment and the blue aquifer is the water table. A broad, shallow
            stream sits in a low bowl on the left, and the water table meets it,
            so shallow groundwater and the stream are one connected system. A
            monitoring well stands beside the stream; a deeper pumping well
            stands away from it. Pumping pulls the water table down into a cone
            of depression and reduces the groundwater that would otherwise reach
            the stream; the gap from the pre-pumping water table is the stream
            depletion attributable to pumping. A model can estimate that
            depletion, but the compliance test runs instead on a groundwater
            level at the monitoring well — a proxy — checked against a
            threshold. That substitution is where the chain breaks.
          </p>

    <p class="isw-phase" aria-hidden="true"><span data-for="physical">Physical response</span><span data-for="accounting">Accounting chain</span></p>
  </div>

  <ol class="gw-steps-scene__steps">
    <li class="gw-step" data-step="pumping" data-phase="physical">
      <span class="gw-step__n">01</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">Pumping</h3>
      <p>Wells pump at different depths. Models see averaged demand spread across grid cells, not individual wells.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="gw-step" data-step="response" data-phase="physical">
      <span class="gw-step__n">02</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">Hydrologic response</h3>
      <p>The water table falls and less groundwater reaches the stream — lagged, attenuated, and mixed with every other driver of streamflow.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="gw-step" data-step="model" data-phase="accounting">
      <span class="gw-step__n">03</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">Measurement &amp; model</h3>
      <p>Every basin runs a numerical model. Three report a pumping-attributable estimate; three report net stream–aquifer exchange from all causes and call it depletion.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="gw-step" data-step="attribution" data-phase="accounting">
      <span class="gw-step__n">04</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">Attribution</h3>
      <p>Runs with and without pumping isolate pumping's share — at basin, reach or zone scale. No basin attributes depletion to individual wells.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="gw-step gw-step--break" data-step="break" data-phase="accounting">
      <span class="gw-step__n">✕</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">The chain breaks</h3>
      <p>Modelled depletion stops here. Compliance switches to a groundwater-level or streamflow proxy, and no basin sets a threshold on a depletion volume.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="gw-step" data-step="threshold" data-phase="accounting">
      <span class="gw-step__n">05</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">Sustainability threshold</h3>
      <p>Five basins set ISW thresholds on groundwater elevations, mostly anchored to a recent drought; Kaweah sets a flow criterion on one reach.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="gw-step" data-step="compliance" data-phase="accounting">
      <span class="gw-step__n">06</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">Accounting &amp; compliance</h3>
      <p>The compliance test runs on that proxy. By the agencies' own account, it cannot separate a pumping effect from a dry year or reservoir operations.</p>
    </li>
    <li class="gw-step" data-step="management" data-phase="accounting">
      <span class="gw-step__n">07</span>
      <h3 class="gw-step__t">Management response</h3>
      <p>Where undesirable results were declared — East Turlock and Salinas Valley — no management consequence followed. The loop back to pumping stays weak.</p>
    </li>
  </ol>
</section>
